newsitem.title: CHILE: Chileans looking at Irish connection to prison break.
newsitem.headline: Chileans looking at Irish connection to prison break.

text.p: Chile's Supreme Court has asked authorities in Ireland for help in investigating a possible link between leftist rebels who fled jail last year and the Irish Republican Army, a newspaper reported on Wednesday.

The Supreme Court sent a 16-page request to Dublin asking for information after two people allegedly involved in the daring helicopter prison escape were found to be Irish citizens and another suspect was Argentine, the newspaper El Mercurio said.
The Supreme Court sent the request for information to the Chilean Foreign Ministry, which would forward it to Irish authorities, in line with formal procedures in such cases, El Mercurio said.
Chilean officials involved in the case had no immediate comment on the report.

The report followed rumours that investigators were looking at an Irish connection to the December 30 crime, in which a helicopter plucked four members of the Manuel Rodriguez Patriotic Front from a prison courtyard.

The escape, which stunned Chileans after years of dormancy by local rebel groups and forced the head of the nation's prison service to resign in disgrace, bore many similarities to an escape by three IRA guerrillas from prison in 1973, said the report.
The Chilean guerrillas had been convicted for a 1986 assassination attempt against then-military ruler Augusto Pinochet and the kidnapping of a newspaper magnate's son and a top rightist politician.

The report in El Mercurio said police had identified two Irishwomen who may be the two foreign-looking women whom witnesses said were involved in groundwork for the escape, including renting the helicopter.

One of the women left Chile within hours of the escape on a Varig flight to Brazil, while the other woman and another suspect fled over the border to Argentina in a rented car, said the report, citing police sources.
Chilean police have already travelled to Ireland and Britain to chase leads there with help from local authorities, the report said.

Officials have long suspected a foreign role in the escape, especially the helicopter's manoeuvre was too skilful for even the best local pilots, but speculation had centred more on Latin American guerrilla groups.

Since the escape occurred only 13 days after Peruvian rebels seized the Japanese ambassador's house in Lima, the two episodes inevitably led to speculation about a revival of the region's now mostly defunct guerrilla bands.
